papers.title_in_file: QML-IDS: Quantum Machine Learning Intrusion Detection System
papers.version_note: arXiv:2410.16308v1 [cs.CR], 7 Oct 2024. The text layer is the six-page preprint with no appended second copy. The paper labels the QCNN column 'QNCC' in Tables II and III and 'QCCN' in Table VII.
papers.what_it_is: A six-page preprint that proposes QML-IDS, a hybrid quantum-classical intrusion detection system, and compares VQC, QSVM and QCNN on three public network security datasets across a noise-free simulator and five IBM backends against SVM, CNN and RF baselines.

existing.note: The stored value restates the authors' sentence and the numbers match Table IV. Table IV lists CNN at 86.72% on UNSW-NB15, above SVM at 82.34%, so the sentence's label 'best performing traditional ML method' does not match the table.
quotes: VQC achieves an F1 score of 88.10% on the UNSW-NB15 dataset, surpassing the best performing traditional ML method, SVM, which scores 82.34%.
existing.certainty_reason: An empirical result from one study.
existing.reader_inference: Table IV gives RF 82.67%, SVM 82.34% and CNN 86.72% on UNSW-NB15, so the best classical value is CNN, not SVM. VQC at 88.10% is still above all three.

quotes: the performance gap between QML and traditional ML methods is not overwhelmingly large, suggesting that while QML offers potential advantages in certain scenarios
traditional ML methods like SVM and RF still hold the upper hand in others.
existing.certainty_reason: An author statement of the paper's own result.
existing.reader_inference: The 'upper hand' sentence sits in the UNSW-NB15 paragraph about Worms and Shellcode; Table V does not show SVM and RF ahead on Worms.

assertions.value: The authors state that QML-IDS is a hybrid network attack detection system that uses both quantum and classical computing, with the quantum and classical parts depending on the QML technique used.
assertions.anchor: Section I and Section IV, p.1-3
quotes: Development of QML-IDS, a QML-based network attack detection system that utilizes both quantum and classical computing.
The Hybrid QML process is then initiated, with the quantum and classical parts according to the QML technique.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors describe their own system design in Sections I and IV.

assertions.value: The authors describe the QML-IDS pipeline as: network monitoring and data collection, feature extraction, data preprocessing, mapping of classical data to quantum states through a feature map, a hybrid quantum-classical learning step, and a classical output used to generate attack alerts.
quotes: QML-IDS begins with network monitoring and data collection, from which features are extracted.
Next, the mapping of classical data to quantum states occurs through the feature map.
The final result of the process is a classical output, an interpretation of the quantum results that is used for the
generation of attack alerts. Based on the analyses performed, the system generates attack alerts whenever suspicious patterns are identified
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV states the pipeline; Figure 2 is the flowchart.
assertions.reader_inference: The evaluation reports offline F1 scores on public datasets; the paper does not report running the monitoring, collection or alert-generation stages.

assertions.value: The authors state that for the VQC the ansatz parameters are adjusted by a classical optimizer, for the QSVM a quantum kernel is generated and used to train the classical prediction model, and for the QCNN the quantum network is generated and optimized classically.
quotes: In the case of VQC, a variational quantum circuit ansatz is generated, whose parameters are adjusted by a classical optimizer.
For QSVM, a quantum kernel is generated, which is used to train the classical prediction model.
In the QCNN, the quantum network is generated and optimized classically.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section IV states how each technique splits quantum and classical work.

assertions.value: The authors state that other hybrid QML methods can also be used in the approach, and that QML-IDS can be implemented partly on a classical system and partly on a quantum system.
quotes: It is important to note that in this approach, other hybrid QML methods can also be used
QML-IDS can then be implemented partly on a classical system and partly on a quantum system.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors state the scope of the proposal in Section IV.

assertions.value: The authors state that the case study uses three network security datasets (UNSW-NB15, CICIDS17 and CICIoT2023) and three classical ML baselines (SVM, CNN and RF), the baselines implemented with the scikit-learn and TensorFlow frameworks, with RF named as the representative classifier to compare with VQC.
quotes: UNSW-NB15 [15], CICIDS17 [16], and CICIoT2023 [17]
Three classical ML methods were selected and will serve as a comparison to the quantum counterparts results
Support Vector Machine (SVM), Convolution Neural Network (CNN), and Random Forest (RF) as a representative classifier to compare with VQC
all implemented using the scikit-learn and TensorFlow frameworks
assertions.certainty_reason: Section V states the datasets and baselines.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not state dataset sizes, train/test splits, sampling, the number of features, the number of qubits, the number of shots, the number of repeated runs, or any variance or confidence interval. It does not state how the classical baselines were tuned. Every reported F1 is a single value.

assertions.value: The authors state that the three QML models (VQC, QSVM and QCNN) were implemented using the Qiskit framework.
quotes: three Quantum Machine Learning models were employed: VQC, QSVM, and QCNN, which were implemented using the Qiskit framework
assertions.certainty_reason: Section V states the implementation framework.

assertions.value: The authors state that four Qiskit feature maps are used to encode classical data into quantum states: RawFeatureVector, PauliFeatureMap, ZFeatureMap and ZZFeatureMap, alongside four ansatz and four classical optimizers.
assertions.anchor: Section V and Table I, p.4
quotes: We employ four feature maps from Qiskit (RawFeatureVector, PauliFeatureMap, ZFeatureMap, ZZFeatureMap)
alongside four Ansatz and classical optimizers within the Qiskit framework
EfficientSU2 ExcitationPreserving
RealAmplitudes TwoLocal Resilience
COBYLA ADAM SPSA
GradientDescent Decoupling
assertions.certainty_reason: Section V and Table I list the hyperparameter space.
assertions.reader_inference: Table I names the ansatz as EfficientSU2, ExcitationPreserving, RealAmplitudes and TwoLocal, and the optimizers as COBYLA, ADAM, SPSA and GradientDescent. The paper does not say which feature map, ansatz or optimizer produced each reported score.

assertions.value: The authors state that the experiments use transpiler optimization levels from 0 to 3, resilience levels 0 (no mitigation) and 1 (readout-error mitigation through Matrixfree Measurement Mitigation), and dynamic decoupling to reduce environmental interactions.
assertions.anchor: Section V and Table I, p.4
quotes: our experiments leverage optimization levels from 0 to 3 for circuit adaptation, with each level introducing increasingly sophisticated optimization strategies, from basic gate collapsing to advanced techniques like peephole optimization and noise-adaptive qubit mapping.
with resilience level 0 offering no mitigation and level 1 targeting readout errors through Matrixfree Measurement Mitigation, alongside dynamic decoupling to reduce environmental interactions
assertions.certainty_reason: Section V states the circuit-level settings; Table I lists their values.

assertions.value: The authors state that the RawFeatureVector offers a direct mapping of classical data to quantum states and establishes a baseline, and that the ZZFeatureMap adds second-order qubit interactions for more complex correlation encoding.
quotes: The RawFeatureVector offers a direct mapping of classical data to quantum states, establishing a baseline.
The ZZFeatureMap extends these capabilities by incorporating second-order qubit interactions for more complex correlation encoding
assertions.certainty_reason: Section V defines the roles of the feature maps.

assertions.value: The authors state that the five real quantum computing environments are IBM CAIRO, IBM KYOTO, IBM BRISBANE, IBM OSAKA and IBM SHERBROOKE, and that these environments incorporate the specific noise models, quantum logic gates and topologies of actual quantum computers.
quotes: IBM CAIRO, IBM KYOTO, IBM BRISBANE, IBM OSAKA, and IBM SHERBROOKE
These environments incorporate the specific noise models, quantum logic gates, and topologies of actual quantum computers
assertions.certainty_reason: Section VI.A names the backends.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper states 'real quantum computing environments' and does not state whether every reported number came from device execution or from a noise-model simulation of the device.

assertions.value: The authors state that the F1 score is chosen for its balanced measure of precision and recall, which they describe as crucial in security contexts for effectively detecting attacks while minimizing false positives.
quotes: The F1 Score is chosen for its balanced measure of precision and recall, crucial in
security contexts for effectively detecting attacks while minimizing false positives.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section VI.A gives the metric and the reason.
assertions.reader_inference: Only F1 is reported. Accuracy, precision, recall, false-positive rate and runtime are not reported.

assertions.value: The authors define the Variational Quantum Classifier as a hybrid QML algorithm that combines parameterized quantum circuits with classical optimization for classification tasks, with three main steps: encoding input data into quantum states, processing them through a variational circuit (ansatz), and optimizing the circuit parameters with classical optimization.
quotes: The Variational Quantum Classifier (VQC) [5] is a hybrid Quantum Machine Learning algorithm that leverages parameterized quantum circuits combined with classical optimization techniques for classification tasks.

The core of the VQC involves three main steps: encoding the input data into quantum states, processing these states through a variational quantum circuit (or Ansatz, Fig 1.b), and optimizing the circuit parameters using classical optimization techniques.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section II.A defines the technique as the paper uses it.

assertions.value: The authors define the Quantum Kernel Support Vector Machine as a quantum-enhanced version of the classical SVM that builds a quantum kernel, a measure of similarity between pairs of data points in a high-dimensional quantum feature space.
quotes: The Quantum Kernel Support Vector Machine (QSVM) [6] represents a quantum-enhanced version of the classical Support Vector Machine (SVM) algorithm
The process involves the construction of a quantum kernel, which is a measure of similarity between pairs of data points in this quantum space.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section II.B defines the technique as the paper uses it.

assertions.value: The authors state that the effectiveness of QSVM heavily relies on the choice of the feature map and the design of the quantum kernel.
quotes: The effectiveness of QSVM heavily relies on the choice of the feature map and the design of the quantum kernel
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement without evidence in the paper; the paper does not isolate the effect of the feature map on any reported score.

assertions.value: The authors define the Quantum Convolutional Neural Network as an adaptation of classical convolutional neural networks, with convolutional layers realized by parameterized unitary operations on neighboring pairs of qubits and pooling achieved by measuring a subset of qubits.
quotes: The Quantum Convolutional Neural Network (QCNN) [7] is an adaptation of classical convolutional neural networks (CNNs).
The convolutional layers in a QCNN are realized through the application of parameterized unitary operations on neighboring pairs of qubits.
is achieved in QCNNs through the measurement of a subset of qubits.
assertions.certainty_reason: Section II.C defines the technique as the paper uses it.

assertions.value: The authors state that the specific choice of feature map influences the VQC's ability to represent the important features of the input data, directly impacting the performance of the generated model.
quotes: the specific choice of the feature map influences
ability to represent the important features of the input data, directly impacting the performance of the generated model.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement without evidence in the paper; no reported score isolates the feature map.

assertions.value: The authors state that NISQ devices are limited in the number of qubits, in circuit complexity (depth and available gates) and in maintaining coherence over time, that NISQ systems lack robust error correction, and that any proposal for a quantum IDS must take these factors into account.
quotes: These limitations include restrictions on the number of qubits (quantum bits) available, the complexity of the quantum circuits that can be implemented (depth and available quantum logic gates)
the lack of robust error correction mechanisms in NISQ systems also represents a
significant obstacle [4]. Therefore, any proposal for a quantum IDS must take these factors into account
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper attributes these limitations to prior surveys (its references 2 to 4).

assertions.value: The authors state that recent advances signify a shift towards the era of quantum utility, in which quantum computers now outperform classical methods in solving complex problems efficiently and accurately, while quantum supremacy has not yet been achieved.
quotes: quantum computers now outperform classical methods in solving complex problems efficiently and accurately [1]
Despite not yet achieving quantum supremacy
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors cite one prior work for this statement.
assertions.reader_inference: The cited work is a utility demonstration on one specific problem; the sentence states it for complex problems in general, and the paper does not show that any task in its own evaluation is beyond classical methods.

assertions.value: The authors state that the experimental results provide empirical evidence of the effectiveness of QML techniques in enhancing network attack detection capabilities and point to the feasibility of implementation in NISQ systems.
quotes: The experimental results provide empirical evidence of the effectiveness of QML techniques in enhancing network attack detection capabilities and point to the feasibility of implementation in NISQ systems.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author summary of their own results.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper's own Section VI.C says the gap to traditional methods is not overwhelmingly large and that QML does not yet decisively outperform them.

assertions.value: The authors report that Said et al. applied a QSVM model to DDoS attack detection in smart micro-grids on a reduced (sampled) version of the CIC-DDoS2019 dataset, and that the results demonstrate the superiority of the QML model compared to the classical SVM.
quotes: Said et al. (2023) [8] explore the application of a QSVM model to detect Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attacks in smart micro-grids.
The study evaluates the QML model using a reduced version (by sampling) of the CIC-DDoS2019 dataset [9]
The results demonstrate the superiority of the QML model compared to the classical approach, SVM.

quotes: the application of a Neural Network (NN) in conjunction with the VQC for network attack detection is proposed

assertions.value: The authors state that the related works by Said et al., Gong et al. and Kalinin and Krundyshev implemented their solutions using noiseless quantum computing simulators, which cannot accurately represent current NISQ systems, whereas their own proposal is implemented using noisy backends.

assertions.value: The authors state that this study expands their earlier work, which tested QML models in a network security context through direct implementation of baseline circuits, by employing quantum circuit optimization techniques alongside more thorough experimentation, and that it covers VQC, QSVM and QCNN for both binary and multiclass scenarios on three datasets.
